Methods for zinbreg fits

Source: R/methods-zinbreg.R
zinbreg-methods.Rd

Standard methods for objects returned by zinbreg(): printing, summaries with coefficient tables for the count and zero parts, extracting coefficients, the variance-covariance matrix, the log-likelihood (with a df attribute, so AIC() and BIC() work), fitted values, residuals, the number of observations, and predictions.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'zinbreg'
print(x, digits = max(3L, getOption("digits") - 3L), ...)

# S3 method for class 'zinbreg'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'summary.zinbreg'
print(x, digits = max(3L, getOption("digits") - 3L), ...)

# S3 method for class 'zinbreg'
coef(object, model = c("full", "count", "zero"), ...)

# S3 method for class 'zinbreg'
vcov(object, model = c("full", "count", "zero"), ...)

# S3 method for class 'zinbreg'
logLik(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'zinbreg'
fitted(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'zinbreg'
residuals(object, type = c("response", "pearson"), ...)

# S3 method for class 'zinbreg'
nobs(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'zinbreg'
predict(
  object,
  newdata,
  type = c("response", "count", "zero", "prob"),
  se.fit = FALSE,
  at = NULL,
  offset = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

x, object

A zinbreg fit (or, for print.summary.zinbreg(), its summary).

digits

Number of significant digits to print.

...

Not used.

model

For coef() and vcov(): "full" (both parts, with names count_* and zero_*), "count" or "zero" (one part, without the prefix), as in pscl::zeroinfl().

type

For residuals(): "response" (\(y - \hat f\), with the fitted mean \(\hat f = (1 - \hat\pi)\hat\mu\)) or "pearson" (the response residual times the square root of the prior weight, divided by the estimated standard deviation \(\sqrt{\hat f (1 + (\hat\pi + 1/\hat\theta)\hat\mu)}\)). For predict(): "response" (the mean \((1 - \pi)\mu\)), "count" (the count-part mean \(\mu\)), "zero" (the structural-zero probability \(\pi\)), or "prob" (the probabilities \(P(Y = k)\) for the counts in at).

newdata

Optional data frame of covariate values for predict(). If omitted, predictions are for the data used in the fit.

se.fit

Logical; if TRUE, predict() also returns standard errors by the delta method (not for type = "prob"). They use the covariance matrix of the count and zero coefficients; theta does not enter these predictions. They are NA for rows that involve a coefficient without a finite estimate.

at

For type = "prob": the counts \(k\) (non-negative whole numbers, without duplicates, in any order) at which to evaluate \(P(Y = k)\); the columns of the result follow this order. The default is 0:max(y), with y the response of the fit.

offset

For predict() with newdata, only when the model was fitted with the offset argument: the count-part offset for the new rows. Offsets written as offset() terms in either part of the formula are always taken from newdata.

Value

coef() a named vector; vcov() a matrix; logLik() an object of class logLik; fitted() and residuals() numeric vectors; nobs() the number of observations with positive weight; predict() a numeric vector (a matrix for type = "prob"), or with se.fit = TRUE a list with elements fit and se.fit; summary() an object of class summary.zinbreg; the print methods return their argument invisibly.

Details

Fitted values, residuals and predictions for the fitted data follow na.action: with stats::na.exclude() they are padded with NA to the length of the original data.

With type = "prob", the result has one row per observation and one column per value of at. To protect against an enormous allocation (for example when the largest count in the data is huge), a result with more than 10 million cells (about 80 MB) is refused with an error that suggests an explicit at.

For new data, the count-part offset follows the rules of predict.nbreg(): offset() terms are evaluated in newdata; an offset argument used in the fit is re-evaluated in newdata when its expression refers to a newdata column, and must otherwise be supplied with offset =. All offsets must be finite.

See also

zinbreg()

Examples

if (requireNamespace("pscl", quietly = TRUE)) {
  data("bioChemists", package = "pscl")
  fit <- zinbreg(art ~ fem + mar + kid5 + phd + ment | ment,
                 data = bioChemists)
  fit
  summary(fit)
  coef(fit, model = "zero")
  AIC(fit)
  nd <- data.frame(fem = "Women", mar = "Married", kid5 = 0, phd = 3,
                   ment = c(0, 10))
  predict(fit, newdata = nd, type = "response", se.fit = TRUE)
  predict(fit, newdata = nd, type = "prob", at = 0:3)
}
#>           0         1         2          3
#> 1 0.5317740 0.2065642 0.1306620 0.06988742
#> 2 0.2535463 0.2727396 0.2013002 0.12563067
